sections.html:
Detroit is the seat of Wayne County and the largest city in Michigan. The 2025 estimate counts 649,095 residents, up from 639,111 in 2020. The county records your deed and holds older delinquent tax accounts, so many sale questions end at a county office rather than at city hall.

A house in Boston-Edison or Indian Village competes in a different market from a modest bungalow elsewhere in the city, even though both pay the same city and county taxes. Price your house against its own block, not against the city as a whole.

Close to half of Detroit households rent, so investors and landlords are a real part of the buyer pool.

A typical owned home at $83,900 beside a typical rent of $1,074 means a rented house can repay its price quickly, which is why investors follow Detroit sales. The same gap makes a roof or furnace replacement a heavy share of a sale price here.

sections.h2: Older houses and what inspectors flag
sections.html:
Beyond downtown and New Center, Detroit is mostly low-rise. Working-class areas built before World War II have wood-frame and brick houses, while Brush Park, Woodbridge, Indian Village, Palmer Woods and Boston-Edison have larger, more ornate homes.

Older houses on clay soil tend to draw the same inspection comments:

  • Furnaces, roofs and plumbing, because the winters are hard on them.
  • Cooling and attic ventilation for the hot weeks.
  • Basement moisture and drainage, since clay holds water against foundations.

Fix these items or price them in before you list.

sections.h2: Who buys and what helps a listing
sections.html:
Midtown's Detroit Medical Center employs more people than anyone else in the city, with Wayne State University beside it and the Henry Ford Health System in New Center. Roughly 80,500 people work downtown, one-fifth of the city's jobs, and buyers who work in those districts look for housing nearby.

Getting around is easier than in many Michigan cities. DDOT buses, the QLINE streetcar and the downtown People Mover loop serve the core, and SMART runs routes to the suburbs. Many families also look at suburban school districts, so ask your agent how school boundaries affect the buyer pool on your street.

Michigan puts its deed tax on the seller. Every $500 block of value carries $3.75 of state tax, and a county layer sits on top: 55 cents per block in a county under two million residents. MCL 207.523, 207.525 and 207.504 set the framework, and the Wayne County deed office confirms the current county rate. You have 15 days from handing over the deed to pay the county treasurer.

MCL 207.526 exempts certain deeds, including a court-ordered transfer with no stated price, a foreclosure deed, and an instrument that creates a joint tenancy where one of the owners already held the property. A lender that later resells a foreclosed house does not get the same break.

  • The buyer reports the transfer to the assessor inside 45 days (MCL 211.27a).
  • For the next calendar year, taxable value is set at the SEV.
  • Ask the Detroit assessor for the form that ends your own principal residence exemption.

For current-year and past-due bill amounts, ask the City of Detroit Office of the Assessor and the Wayne County Treasurer for written payoff figures before you sign anything.

sections.h2: Selling before a tax foreclosure auction
sections.html:
The Wayne County Treasurer, whose office is at 400 Monroe Street in Detroit, holds an annual online auction of tax-foreclosed properties. The minimum bid is a fixed amount that includes the treasurer's foreclosure and auction costs. Winners have 72 hours to pay in full, and the office records a quit claim deed within 30 days after the auction closes.

Selling before the auction lets you choose the buyer and the price. Call the treasurer and ask what redemption rights remain on your parcel and whether a payment plan is available. Have the closing agent settle any balance from your proceeds, since a buyer's lender expects the lien cleared when the deed changes hands.

sections.h2: Comparing offers on a house that needs work
sections.html:
Three questions decide most Detroit sales: what an appraiser will accept, what an inspector will list, and what taxes are still open on the parcel. A mortgage buyer needs all three to line up. An investor offer skips the appraisal, and an as-is contract can say who clears trash, personal property and open utility accounts.

Line up offers by what you walk away with: price, minus deed tax, minus unpaid taxes and liens, minus repairs you would otherwise fund. Ask each bidder for evidence of funds and a dated closing plan before you choose.

A cash sale skips the lender's appraisal and most repair requests, which matters when the house has a worn roof, old plumbing or damp basement. Whatever route you pick, gather the payoff letters first so nothing about the liens surprises you after you sign.

sections.h2: What to gather before you list
sections.html: Put together your deed information, recent tax bills and a note of any open utility accounts. If the house is a rental, ask the City of Detroit what compliance rules apply to your property type and whether anything is outstanding. Request written payoff figures from the City of Detroit Office of the Assessor and the Wayne County Treasurer. With those papers in hand, a buyer or closing agent can move quickly, and you can compare offers on real numbers instead of guesses.

sections.h2: What happens at a Detroit closing
sections.html:
The closing agent reads the payoff letters, subtracts the deed tax and any liens from the price, and sends you the remainder. The deed is recorded with Wayne County, and the buyer then reports the transfer to the assessor. If you had a principal residence exemption, file the form that ends it so the new owner's bill is set correctly.

Walk through the house before closing and clear out trash and personal property, since an as-is contract usually makes that the seller's job. Settle open utility accounts on the day you hand over the keys. A sale where the buyer pays cash and accepts the house as it is tends to close with fewer of these loose ends, because no lender is waiting on an appraisal or a repair list.

faqs.q: Which side owes the state deed tax on a Detroit house?
faqs.a: The seller. Michigan names the grantor as the liable party. The state takes $3.75 on each $500 block, Wayne County adds its portion, and a court-ordered transfer without a stated price is among the exempt deeds.

faqs.q: Can a Detroit house with unpaid taxes still be sold?
faqs.a: Yes. Request an official payoff letter from the Wayne County Treasurer and let the closing agent settle it out of your proceeds. Selling ahead of the county's foreclosure auction keeps the choice of buyer with you.

faqs.q: How does a sale change the Detroit tax bill?
faqs.a: The buyer's taxable value is reset for the next year to the SEV, the figure the assessor sets at half of market value. The buyer reports the transfer to the assessor inside 45 days.

faqs.q: Must I repair my Detroit house before selling?
faqs.a: Buyers and their lenders often ask for repairs, and the contract decides who pays. Ask the City of Detroit about any compliance rules that apply to your property type, especially a rental.

faqs.q: How many people live in Detroit, and what do homes sell for?
faqs.a: The 2025 estimate counts 649,095 residents. For 2020 to 2024 the middle price of an owned house is $83,900, and about one home in two has its owner living inside.
